content.title: Review
content.review:
***Summary***
The paper presents a model to keep the hyper-spherical energy of the linear layer of a network low. It argues that this is beneficial for the generalisation of the models. The authors show experiments to back up this assertion.

This paper explores the idea of fixing a matrix $A$ and optimising $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(n)$ in the expression $QA$, and use $QA$ as the linear kernel of a linear layer.

***Comments***

On overparametrisation.

I do not see how this method accounts for an overparametrisation of the layer. This paper substitutes a linear layer $n^2$ parameters with an orthogonal layer $n(n-1)/2$ parameters. At the same time, in section 6.3 the authors day that an OPT network has $\times 5$ the parameters as the original network. Could the authors expand on this?

On the optimisation with orthogonal constraints.

The paper spends a page and a half out of the eight describing different optimisation methods for orthogonal constraints. This is completely tangential to the point of the paper, given that the paper does not introduce any new optimisation method. At the same time, as explained in appendix M, CP is the optimisation method that is most efficient and performs best. Why did the authors use GS in many of the experiments? Using just CP would be much more efficient and it would save them 1 page of explanations.

On the importance of the hyperspherical energy.

The paper is claims in several places that the hyperspherical energy "improves generalisation" in neural networks. The authors put their method at the level of other well known theoretical papers in section 5.2. On the other hand, I do not think that this comparison is valid as it is, as these other papers study very specific forms of neural networks. I think that, if the authors are going to make these claims, they should show how their method can be proven to have the same advantages as the cited ones via some corollary of their theories.

On the CNNs.

The exposition of the definition of hyperspherical energy is always done for linear layers, but almost all the experiments are performed in CNN networks. It is not very clear to me how does one define the HE for a tensor. I think that this should be explained in the main paper. Could the authors expand on this?

On the experiments.
- In the first experiment the authors claim that doing OPT with GS works better than doing unconstrained optimisation. Could the authors explain this?
- We see the application of OPT to Few-shot learning, improving over a previous experiment. On the other hand, we see that the improvement is marginal, and the variance says that it is not significant. It is not clear whether the little improvement gained over the initial method comes from the framework or simply from having a model with multiple times the parameters of the original model.
- In the experiment "Fixed weights vs. learnable weights" the authors claim that this proves that OPT is beneficial to generalisation, without providing the any sort of validation loss!

***Conclusion:***
This paper proposes a framework where linear layers are reparametrised via a fixed matrix and an orthogonal trainable matrix. It is not clear to me how to apply this to CNNs or how this is an overparametrised network. In general, I do not think that this is going to be a practical method that can be used in practice. In particular, I do not like that the experiments just get a marginal improvement over their baselines while using 4-5 times the parameters. S-OPT comes to solve this, but it is just evaluated in one experiment, when it the authors could have added it as an extra experiment in every of their previous experiments.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Thanks for the review!
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for the review! We are delighted to address these questions.

-- Overparametrisation

Our overparametrisation is in two folds. (1) each neuron is linearly factorized into an orthogonal matrix and a vector. (2) the orthogonal matrix itself is an overparameterization. Eg, in CNN, 32 neurons of size $3\times3\times16$ have 4.6K params, while OPT has 20K params for this layer in training (see Sect 4.2). 

The authors may have misunderstandings about our paper. Even for linear layers, OPT is also over-parameterizing the neurons if the dimension of neurons ($d$) is (much) larger than the number of neurons ($n$). This is in fact very common in practice. Since the training parameters for OPT is $d(d-1)/2$ while the typical linear layer contains $dn$ training parameters.

-- Optimization

Thanks for the suggestion. We comprehensively compare different orthogonalization in OPT, and evaluate how these different methods generalize in different task. This is one of our contribution. Indeed, using CP is more efficient in practice, but it only covers a subset of the orthogonal group, unlike G-S. Besides, different orthogonalizations yield different inducitve biases, as shown in our experiments. We think it is of sufficient interest to compare them. We will try to make this section more concise, but we believe it is also important to make our paper self-contained.

-- Hyperspherical Energy

[67] theoretically shows MHE can improve SGD optimization and generalization (OPT theoretically matches the assumption that neurons are uniformly distributed on hypersphere). [45] empirically demonstrate MHE yields better generalization on many tasks. OPT is motivated by these work. Justifications are also in Section 4 & Appendix D,E,J. We agree that having more theoretical evidence to support our claim is important, and it definitely falls in our future investigation. But the focus of this paper is not pure theory. Our current paper aims to propose a general training framework that provably minimizes the hyperspherical energy during training.

-- CNN

The authors may need to view both MLP and CNN from a neuron perspective. It means that one layer in both MLP and CNN is constructed by multiple neurons. Applying OPT to CNN is similar to MLP, because a convolutional neuron is simply a mapping from a receptive field to a real number. MLP can be viewed as a special CNN with kernel having the same size as the input feature map. 

-- GS

GS vs. unconstrained optimizaiton is basically applying orthogonality to the transformation matrices vs. no constraints on the transformation matrices. It indicates that using orthogonal matrices to transform the neurons (which can also preserve the small hyperspherical energy) is beneficial to generalization.

-- Few-shoe learning

Our main goal is not few-shot learning. Few-shot learning is simply one application that showcases that OPT is able to achieve better generalization than baselines. The experiments show that using OPT to train neural networks in few-shot settings may also be beneificial. Besides that, the improvement is very consistent, since we run OPT many times and it can perform better than baseline in every run.

-- S-OPT

S-OPT is especially designed for large-scale settings. Since all the previous experiments can use the original OPT, there is no need to use S-OPT. Moreover, we have already compared one of the previous setting for S-OPT and OPT in CNN-6 case in Table 8. Of course it is easy to supplement S-OPT in all the previous results. We will do that in revision.

display_title: Review: Interesting idea, but some concerns.

content.title: Review: Interesting idea, but some concerns.
content.review:
### Summary 
**Objective:** improve generalization of neural networks by attaining small hyperspherical energy. 

**Approach:** initialize neurons so hyperspherical energy is provably low in a probabilistic sense. Then, optimize an orthogonal transformation of the neurons weights, instead of optimizing the weights of the neurons. The orthogonal transformation does not change hyperspherical energy, so the trained network retains the same low hyperspherical energy it had at initialization. 

### Strengths
**[+]** Optimizing an orthogonal transformation instead of neuron weights is interesting.

**[+]** Experiments seem to indicate consistent improvements in generalization, relative to baseline networks and networks with orthogonal weights (see Table 4). 

**[+]** Using orthogonal matrices to preserve lower initial hyperspherical energy is quite clever. 

### Weaknesses
**[-]** Writing. It was hard for me to understand the key points of the paper. 

**[-]** The article spends 1.5 pages covering previous work in section 3 which presents their work.  

**[-]** It seems to me there are a few statements that are misleading bordering to wrong (not anything relating to main idea), see Concern 1 and Concern 3. 

**[-]** Over-parameterized is defined differently in the referenced work, e.g., [1, 42]. It think the paper would be more clear if such differences were clarified, especially since 'over-parameterized' is in the title of the article. Please note that [1] clarify what they mean by over-parameterization in their abstract and [42] clarify what they mean by over-parameterization in the second line of their introduction.

**[-]** For fully connected networks the time of evaluating a layer increase from $O(n^2 \cdot \text{batch size})$ to $O(n^3)$. Typically $n>>\text{batch size}$. This seems to be a big drawback. While section 4 attempts to address this issue, I do not believe the issue is properly explained and clarified for the reader. 

### Recommendation: Leaning towards rejection 5

**[+]** Optimizing an orthogonal transformation instead of neuron weights is interesting (main reason I did not give 4).  

**[-]** Writing. I think there is a lot of opportunity to help future readers of this paper. 

**[-]** For fully connected networks the time of evaluating a layer increase from $O(n^2 \cdot \text{batch size})$ to $O(n^3)$. Typically $n>>\text{batch size}$. This seems to be a big drawback. While section 4 attempts to address this issue, I do not believe the issue is properly explained and clarified for the reader. 

I am open to changing my recommendation if the authors address the questions/concerns below. That said, I'll first re-evaluate my opinion based on the comments from the other reviews. It is likely that I missed things the other reviewers caught. 

### Questions and Concerns

Question 1. How is over-parameterization defined in [1, 12, 16, 31, 42], how do the definitions differ, and how would the authors define over-parameterization? 

The article cite [1, 12, 16, 31, 42] which contain different definitions of 'over-parameterization'. For example: 

[1] defines over-parameterization when network width is polynomially large in the number of layers L and the number of samples n. 

[42] defines over-parameterization as "the technique of using more parameters than statistically necessary". 

By the definition in [1] OPT is not over-parameterized, but by the definition in [42] OPT would typically be over-parameterized. You later write "In this light, OPT also introduces over-parameterization to each neuron ... ". This is true/false depending on which definition of over-parameterized you are using. 

I apologize if I am misunderstanding previous work. If that is the case, perhaps it would be a good idea to clarify this in the related work. Alternatively, one might attempt to make such statements more precise. 

Concern 1. You write that "Givens rotations can also construct the orthogonal matrix, ..., which takes $O(n^2)$ complexity and is too costly". The matrix-vector multiplication used in your OPT approach also take $O(n^2)$ time for each neuron, so I do not understand why $O(n^2)$ is too costly. I think the main issue with Givens rotations is lack of parallelization and not time complexity. 

If I am wrong, please explain why, if not, please explain how you will clarify the issue. 

Concern 2. In section 4 you write "If the dimension of neurons become is extremely large, then the orthogonal matrix to transform the neurons will also be large. Therefore, it may take large GPU memory and time to train the neural network with the original OPT. "
First of, I think you need to remove "is" or "become" from this sentence. Second, in fully connected networks, the memory requirements increase from $n^2$ to $n^2+n(n-1)/2<2n^2$ while time consumption increase from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n^3)$ if you have $n$ input/output neurons. I don't think this is clear from context and it could be clarified. 

Concern 3. Consider, for example, the sentence "... , all OPT variants maintain minimal energy in training. ". To me, this sounds like OPT attains the global minimal hyperspherical energy, which, in general, is false. To me, this seems to be overselling the method a bit. This happens a few times through-out the article, and I recommend you make such statements more precise, e.g., " ..., all OPT variants maintain much lower hypherspherical energy during training. ".  

Concern 4.  In the introduction I think the wording "strong interpretability" is misleading and over claiming, I suggest to only write "flexibility". 

Concern 5. Sections 3.3 - 3.6 seems to cover related work, but is presented in the section describing your method. I think this could be removed, or moved to the related work section in a very condensed form. This would make it more clear what is your work and what is previous work. Finally, it seems to me that your key idea is minimization of hyperspherical energy by using orthogonal matrices, therefore, it doesn't seem important exactly how you use orthogonal matrices, just that it can be done without increasing training time too much. The details might even be removed to appendix. 

### Additional Feedback

Comment 1. It seems to me that uniformly sampling neurons as done in section 4 resembles dropout. If this is the case, I think you may be able to use column-row-sampling instead, which has provable guarantees wrt. Frobenious norm which dropout does not. 

Comment 2. I think it is possible to shorten the abstract, and thus help future readers get a clear understanding of your idea. For example, the first sentence with inductive biases could be completely removed, so future readers get to the main point faster. I think the second sentence could be rephrased. 

Comment 3. In the introduction you cite [15] two times ```[15,15,16,31,42]```.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Thank you for your review!
content.comment:
Thank you for these questions and concerns. We are deeply appreciative your comments, since they can greatly help us improve the paper.

Question 1: "How is over-parameterization defined in [1, 12, 16, 31, 42], how do the definitions differ, and how would the authors define over-parameterization?"

Response: We agree with the reviewer that over-parameterization has a broad set of definitions. The essence would be "using more parameters than necessary". Over-parameterization in OPT particularly corresponses to the training process and how we conduct inference for the OPT-trained neural networks. This is because OPT will multiply the orthogonal matrices back to the neurons, such that the OPT-trained networks have the same number of parameters with the baseline. We view these orthogonal matrices as "additional" training parameters. In terms of a single neuron, it will be a vevtor multiplied by a large orthogonal matrix, so this is the reason why we understand it as "over-parameterized training". We agree with the reviewer that we can make this statement more precisely. Therefore, we will discuss this further in our paper to clarify potential misunderstandings. Overall, we think it is mostly a very minor problem which does not affect the correctness of our method.

Concern 1: "You write that "Givens rotations can also construct the orthogonal matrix, ..., which takes $O(n^2)$ complexity and is too costly". The matrix-vector multiplication used in your OPT approach also take $O(n^2)$ time for each neuron, so I do not understand why $O(n^2)$ is too costly. I think the main issue with Givens rotations is lack of parallelization and not time complexity."

Response: The reason Givens rotation is computationally expensive is in two folds. First, the dimension of neurons in CNNs can go up to more than 1000 (e.g., 3x3x128), and this means a matrix of 1000 by 1000. Then unrolling Givens takes $O(d^2)$ steps. The time complexity for it is way higher than the other approaches. Second, the GPU memory consumption is also too costly for Givens rotation, since unrolling more steps will also require gradient back-propagation where the gradients need to be stored in GPU memory.

Concern 2: "In section 4 you write "If the dimension of neurons become is extremely large, then the orthogonal matrix to transform the neurons will also be large. Therefore, it may take large GPU memory and time to train the neural network with the original OPT. " First of, I think you need to remove "is" or "become" from this sentence. Second, in fully connected networks, the memory requirements increase from $n^2$ to $n^2+n(n-1)/2<2n^2$ while time consumption increase from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n^3)$ if you have  input/output neurons. I don't think this is clear from context and it could be clarified."

Response: Sorry for not being clear enough. We will include more details to clarify this section in revision.

Concern 3: "Consider, for example, the sentence "... , all OPT variants maintain minimal energy in training. ". To me, this sounds like OPT attains the global minimal hyperspherical energy, which, in general, is false. To me, this seems to be overselling the method a bit. This happens a few times through-out the article, and I recommend you make such statements more precise, e.g., " ..., all OPT variants maintain much lower hypherspherical energy during training. "."

Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We will revise our paper accordingly.

Concern 4: "In the introduction I think the wording "strong interpretability" is misleading and over claiming, I suggest to only write "flexibility"."

Response: Thanks for the suggestion. We will revise it accordingly.

Concern 5: "Sections 3.3 - 3.6 seems to cover related work, but is presented in the section describing your method. I think this could be removed, or moved to the related work section in a very condensed form. This would make it more clear what is your work and what is previous work. Finally, it seems to me that your key idea is minimization of hyperspherical energy by using orthogonal matrices, therefore, it doesn't seem important exactly how you use orthogonal matrices, just that it can be done without increasing training time too much. The details might even be removed to appendix."

Response: We agree with the reviewer that these sections can be more clearly presented. We will try to arrange them a bit to emphasize our contributions.

display_title: A novel training pipeline, but experiments can be improved

content.title: A novel training pipeline, but experiments can be improved
content.review:
This paper proposes an orthogonal over-parameterized training (OPT) framework for neural networks. The motivation of this framework is to minimize the hyperspherical energy to diversify the neurons on a hypersphere, so as to enable better generalization of the network. The idea is simple that OPT fixes the randomly initialized weights of the neuron and learns an orthogonal matrix R that mutiplies to those new neurons. To maintain the orthogonality of the matrix R during the training, several approaches can be adopted, such as unrolling orthogonalization algorithms, orthogonal parameterization and orthogonality-preserving gradient descent. To make it scalable, the author proposes a stochastic version of the training pipeline (S-OPT), in which the some dimensions of the neurons in the same layer are selected and construct a small orthogonal matrix to transform these dimensions together. Such a stochastic algorithm is also shown to preserve the hyperspherical energy of the neurons. Empirical studies show that OPT can improve several neural network baselines (multilayer perceptron, convolution networks) on different datasets (CIFAR-100, Imaginet).  

Overall, the contribution of this paper is to propose a novel training pipeline that can preserve the orthogonality fo the network, which seems to improve the generalization.

Here are some comments:

1. Why do you list methods from section 3.3 to 3.5. They seem to be the classical algorithms in the literature but not the even used in the experiment. If my understanding is correct, what is used is the formulation in sec 3.6, which is an unconstraint optimization problem and are much easier to solve.

2. In the experiments, the baselines are not very strong. 
	a) only a 6-layer or 9-layer CNN is used for CIFAR-100, and the results are very far away from state-of-the-art. 
	b) Also, only a 3-layer MLP is adopted for MNIST.
	c) the imagenet error rate is also quite high.

Although I don’t think it is necessary to pursue state-of-the-art to show the value of the proposed method, I believe using relatively up-to-date neural networks to show improvement is more convincing.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

replying_to: Replying to A novel training pipeline, but experiments can be improved

content.title: Thank you for your review!
content.comment:
Thanks for the suggestion! We are happy to answer your questions.


Concern 1: "Why do you list methods from section 3.3 to 3.5. They seem to be the classical algorithms in the literature but not the even used in the experiment. If my understanding is correct, what is used is the formulation in sec 3.6, which is an unconstraint optimization problem and are much easier to solve."

Response: The reviewer may misunderstand our paper. In fact, we have experimented all the methods proposed in these sections and empirically compared them in a comprehensive way. Please see our experiment section for detailed results.


Concern 2: "In the experiments, the baselines are not very strong. a) only a 6-layer or 9-layer CNN is used for CIFAR-100, and the results are very far away from state-of-the-art. b) Also, only a 3-layer MLP is adopted for MNIST. c) the imagenet error rate is also quite high."

Response: Thanks for the suggestion. In fact, we have used both VGG-like plain neural networks and residual networks to evaluate our method. As emphasized in the paper, we are focusing more on the apple-to-apple comparison. Therefore, our experiments are fair in the sense that both baseline and our method use exactly the same experimental settings. 

To further address your concerns, we conduct an empirical evaluation on DenseNet-121. Our experiments show that OPT can achieve ~24.9% top-1 accuracy, in comparison to the baseline that achieves 25.5% top-1 accuracy.

display_title: We thank all the reviewers for the constructive reviews!

content.title: We thank all the reviewers for the constructive reviews!
content.comment:
Dear reviewers and ACs,

We are sorry that we decide to withdraw our paper and submit to another venue, because we have done a major revision to our paper. It will be more fair to have another round of reviews.

Thank you so much for all these constrcutive suggestions to improve our paper. We will take every comment seriously and revise our paper accordingly. We are deeply appreciative for your time and efforts!

We are also thankful for the recognition on our *novelty*, since all the reviewers agree that our proposed training pipeline is interesting and of sufficient novelty. We will definitely further improve our paper!

Best,
Authors
